There Nearchus sacrificed to Zeus the Saviour and held a contest of athletics.37.1. When the rites had been performed by him in due order, then they put out. Coasting past a desert and rugged island, they anchored at another island, this large and inhabited, having sailed three hundred stades from where they set out.

The desert island was called Organa, and the one at which they anchored Oaracta. Vines grew in it, and date-palms, and it bore grain; the length of the island was eight hundred stades. And the governor of the island, Mazenes, sailed with them as far as Susa, a willing guide of the voyage.
In this island they said that the tomb of the first ruler of this country was shown; his name was Erythres, from whom this sea too has its name.

Setting out from there they sailed on; and having coasted along the island about two hundred stades, they anchored at it again, and observed another island, distant from this great one about forty stades. It was said to be sacred to Poseidon, and not to be set foot upon.

Toward dawn they put out, and an ebb so strong caught them that three of the ships ran aground and were held on the dry land, while the others with difficulty got through the surf and came safe into the deeps.
The ships that had run aground, when the flood came on, floated off again, and on the next day came in to where the whole fleet lay.
They anchored at another island, distant from the mainland about three hundred stades, having sailed four hundred.

From there toward dawn they sailed, passing a desert island on their left; the name of the island was Pylora. And they anchored at Sisidone, a small town and destitute of all things save water and fish; for these too were Fish-eaters by necessity, since they hold a poor land.
From there, having watered, they put in to Tarsias, a headland reaching out into the open sea, having sailed three hundred stades. From there to Cataea, a desert island, low-lying;
this was said to be sacred to Hermes and Aphrodite; the length of the voyage was three hundred stades.

To this island each year sheep and goats are sent by the people round about, sacred to Hermes and Aphrodite, and these were to be seen run wild through time and desolation.38.1. As far as this point is Carmania; the parts from here on the Persians hold. The length of the voyage along the country of the Carmanians is three thousand seven hundred stades. They live like the Persians, since they border on the Persians; and they array themselves for war in the same way.

Setting out from there they sailed now along Persia, and put in to a place called Ila, where there is a harbour by a small and desert island; the name of the island is Caïcandrus, and the voyage three hundred stades.

Toward dawn, sailing to another island, they anchored, and it was inhabited; there too, Nearchus says, pearls are fished, as in the Indian sea. Coasting along the headland of this island about forty stades, there they anchored.
From there they anchored by a high mountain—Ochus was the name of the mountain—in a harbour with good anchorage, and fishermen dwelt there.
And from there, having sailed four hundred and fifty stades, they anchored at Apostana; and many boats lay there at anchor, and there was a village distant sixty stades from the sea.

Putting out from there by night, they sailed into a gulf settled with many villages. The length of the voyage was four hundred stades; and they anchored by the foot of a mountain. There many date-palms grew, and all such other fruit-trees as grow in Greece.

Setting out from there they coasted to Gogana, about six hundred stades, to an inhabited country; and they anchored at the mouths of a winter torrent—its name was Areon. There they anchored with difficulty; for the entrance at the mouth was narrow, since the ebb made the parts around it shallow.

And from there again they anchored at the mouth of another river, having sailed through about eight hundred stades; the name of the river was Sitacus. But neither here did they anchor easily, and this whole voyage along Persia was through shallows and surf and shoals.

There they found much grain gathered together by command of the king, that they might provision themselves; and there they stayed in all twenty-one days, and hauling up the ships, repaired such of them as had been damaged, and tended the rest.39.1. Setting out from there they came to the city Hieratis, an inhabited place. The voyage was seven hundred and fifty stades; and they anchored in a canal led from the river into the sea, whose name was Heratemis.
At sunrise they coasted to a winter torrent, named Padargus, and the whole place was a peninsula. And in it were many gardens and fruit-trees of every kind; the name of the place was Mesambria.

Setting out from Mesambria and sailing through about two hundred stades, they anchored at Taoce, on the river Granis. And from this up the river were the royal palaces of the Persians, distant from the mouths of the river about two hundred stades.
During this coasting voyage Nearchus says that a sea-monster was seen cast up upon the shore, and that some of the sailors, sailing up to it, measured it and said it was fifty cubits.

Its skin was scaly, so deep that it stood out even a cubit; and it had oysters and limpets and much seaweed growing upon it. And he says that many dolphins were to be seen about the monster, and the dolphins larger than those in the inner sea.
Setting out from there they put in to the Rhogonis, a winter torrent, in a harbour with good anchorage; the length of the coasting voyage was two hundred stades.

From there, having sailed through four hundred stades, they bivouacked by a winter torrent; Brizana was the name of the river. There they anchored with difficulty, because there was surf and shallows, and rocks rose out of the sea. But when the flood came on, then they anchored;
and when the water ebbed, the ships were left on the dry. But when the flood, returning in its turn, came up again, then, putting out, they anchored at a river;

the name of the river was Oroatis. The greatest of the rivers, as Nearchus says, of all that on this coasting voyage discharge into the outer sea.40.1. As far as this point the Persians dwell; the parts from here on the Susians hold. And above the Susians another independent people dwells alongside them; they are called the Uxians, of whom I have said in my other work that they are robbers. The length of the coasting voyage along the country of Persia is four thousand four hundred stades.
The land of Persia is said to be divided into three by its climates. The part of it settled by the Red Sea is sandy and barren by reason

of the heat; but the parts from there going toward the north and the north wind are well-tempered in their climate, and the country is grassy, with watered meadows, and bears much vine and all other fruits, except the olive;

and it blooms with parks of every kind, and is watered by clear rivers and lakes, and is good for all the birds whose haunts are about rivers and lakes, and good for horses, and pastures the other beasts of burden, and is in many places wooded and full of game.

But the part still farther on, going toward the north, is wintry and snowy, so that Nearchus says certain envoys from the Euxine Sea, having travelled a very short road, met Alexander on the road as he went through Persia, to his astonishment, and told Alexander of the shortness of the way.
That the Uxians are neighbours to the Susians I have said, just as the Mardians dwell next to the Persians, robbers these too, and the Cossaeans next to the Medes.
And all these peoples Alexander tamed, falling upon them in the winter season, when they reckoned their country impassable.

And he founded cities, that they should be no longer nomads but tillers and workers of the soil, and should have something for which they might fear to do one another harm. From there the army passed along the land of the Susians.
And these things too Nearchus no longer reports with the same accuracy that he is able to describe, except indeed the anchorages and the length of the voyage;
for the country was for the most part full of shoals and reaching far out into the sea with surf, and so unsafe to anchor at. So their passage was for the most part out in the open sea.

They set out from the mouths of the river where they had bivouacked on the borders of Persia, and took aboard water for five days; for the pilots of the voyage said there was no water.41.1. Having been carried five hundred stades, they anchored at the mouth of a lake full of fish, whose name was Cataderbis; and there was a little island at the mouth, Margastana the name of the islet.

From there toward dawn, putting out, they were carried through the shallows in single file; on this side and that, stakes were fixed to mark out the shallows, just as in the channel between the island of Leucas and Acarnania signs are set up for sailors, that the ships may not run aground on the shoals.

But the shoals by Leucas, being sandy, allow those who run aground a quick refloating; but here on either side of the channel there is mud, deep and slimy, so that for those who ran aground there was no contrivance by which to be saved.
For the poles, sinking into the mud, were of no help to them, and for the men to get out and push the ships off into the channel was impossible; for they sank into the mud up to the breast.
So, having with difficulty got through about six hundred stades, each ship anchoring by itself, there they took thought of their meal.

By night now they sailed through the deeps, and the next day until the unyoking of the oxen at evening; and they came nine hundred stades, and came to anchor at the mouth of the Euphrates by a certain village of the land of Babylonia—its name was Diridotis—
where the merchants bring frankincense from the country round about, and all the other spices that the land of Arabia bears.

From the mouth of the Euphrates as far as Babylon Nearchus says there are about three thousand three hundred stades.42.1. There it was announced that Alexander was setting out for Susa. Whereupon they too sailed back, that, sailing up the river Pasitigris, they might join Alexander.
So they sailed the opposite way, keeping the land of Susiana on their left, and coasted past a lake, into which the river Tigris discharges,
which, flowing from Armenia past the city Ninus—once long ago great and prosperous—shuts off the land in the middle between itself and the river Euphrates, which is from this called Mesopotamia.

From the lake to the river itself is six hundred stades, where there is also a village of Susiana which they call Aginis; and this is distant from Susa about five hundred stades. The length of the coasting voyage along the land of the Susians as far as the mouth of the river Pasitigris is two thousand stades.

From there they sailed up the Pasitigris through a country inhabited and prosperous. And having sailed up about a hundred and fifty stades, they anchored, waiting for those whom Nearchus had sent to find out where the king was.
He himself sacrificed to the saving gods, and held a contest, and the whole naval army was in good cheer.
When it was announced that Alexander was now approaching, they sailed again up the river; and they anchored by the bridge of boats on which Alexander was about to bring his army across to Susa.

There the two armies were joined, and sacrifices were offered by Alexander for the safety of the ships and the men, and contests were held; and wherever Nearchus appeared among the army, he was pelted with flowers and ribbons.

There too Nearchus and Leonnatus were crowned with golden crowns by Alexander—Nearchus for the safety of the fleet, Leonnatus for the victory which he won over the Oritae and the barbarians who dwell beside the Oritae. So the army, setting out from the mouths of the Indus, came safe through to Alexander.43.1. The parts on the right of the Red Sea, beyond Babylonia, are the greater part of Arabia; and of this, part reaches down to the sea by Phoenicia and Palestine Syria, while toward the setting sun, as far as the inner sea, the Egyptians border on Arabia.

By Egypt a gulf running in from the great sea makes it plain that, in respect of the outer sea being all one water, there would be a way round by sea from Babylon into this gulf that runs in toward Egypt.
But in fact no man has ever sailed along here, by reason of the heat and the desolation, save some who were carried out in the open sea.
But those of the army of Cambyses who came safe from Egypt to Susa, and those sent by Ptolemy the son of Lagus to Seleucus Nicator at Babylon,

passing through a certain isthmus of the land of Arabia, traversed in eight days in all a waterless and desert country, driving hard upon camels and carrying water for themselves on the camels, and travelling by night; for by day they were unable to bear the open air on account of the heat.

So far is the country beyond this region—which we have shown to be an isthmus running down from the Arabian gulf to the Red Sea—from being inhabited, that the parts of it reaching farther toward the north are desert and sandy.

But men setting out from the Arabian gulf by Egypt, sailing round the greater part of Arabia in order to come to the sea by Susa and Persia, sailed along Arabia as far as the water aboard their ships held out, and then returned home again.
But those whom Alexander sent from Babylon, to sail as far as possible on the right of the Red Sea and learn the regions there, examined some islands lying along the coasting voyage,
and perhaps put in too at the mainland of Arabia; but the headland which lies over against it none was able to pass and bend round to the farther side.
But I think that, if it had been navigable and passable that way, it would have been proved navigable and passable by Alexander’s restless energy.

Hanno the Libyan, setting out from Carthage, sailed out beyond the Pillars of Heracles into the outer sea, keeping Libya on his left; and his voyage was toward the rising sun for thirty-five days in all;
but when he turned south, he met with many perplexities—want of water, and burning heat, and streams of fire pouring into the sea.

But Cyrene, settled in the more desolate parts of Libya, is grassy and well-watered and full of fruits of every kind and of cattle, as far as where the silphium grows; but beyond the silphium the upper parts of it are desert and sandy. Let this account of mine be set down,
bearing, this too, on Alexander the son of Philip, the Macedonian.
